html:
The big picture

The lecture puts conservation of energy from 11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy to work and then opens a second conservation law. (1) A falling rock trades potential energy for kinetic energy; the total stays m g h at every height. (2) Two slides of the same height give the same final speed, whatever their shape; only the arrival time depends on the shape (the cycloid is fastest). (3) A bungee jumper needs gravity and a spring energy \tfrac12 k\,\Delta y^2 together; energy conservation gives a quadratic equation for the lowest point. (4) With friction, mechanical energy turns into heat, F_F\cdot x, which limits how far a block can slide: x_\max = H/\mu. (5) Energy and power units: J, N·m, W·s, calorie, kWh. (6) In a crash the forces are huge and unknown. Instead the lecture uses linear momentum \vec p = m\vec v, which, by Newton's third law, is conserved in every collision. Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic collision; in a (fully) inelastic collision the bodies stick together.

1 Energy conservation: the falling rock

Lecture: p. 5 (from "NOVEMBER 6") · Giancoli §8-3, §8-4

Pasted figure: a man on a stool holds a rock at height y_1 = h ("all potential energy"); halfway down the rock has "half PE, half KE"; at y_2 = 0 it has "all kinetic energy". Bar charts beside each position show PE (blue) and KE (red). The y axis points up from the floor.

Three positions (board): I at y = h; II at 0 < y < h; III at h = y = 0 … meaning the floor, y = 0. The rock starts from rest at I. Only gravity acts (air resistance neglected), a conservative force, so the mechanical energy must stay constant. The lecture checks this at each position.

At I the rock is at rest: only potential energy.

E_\text{pot} = m_\text{Rock}\cdot g\cdot h

At II it has fallen h - y and has both forms. Its speed after a drop h - y is the free-fall result v = \sqrt{2gh} with h replaced by the drop height (5 Uniformly Accelerated Motion and Free Fall):

E_\text{pot} = m_\text{Rock}\cdot g\cdot y, \qquad E_\text{kin} = m_\text{Rock}\cdot\frac{v_\text{Rock}^2}{2}, \qquad v_\text{Rock} = \sqrt{2g\,(h - y)}
E_\text{kin} = m_\text{Rock}\cdot\frac{\left(\sqrt{2g\,(h-y)}\right)^2}{2} = m_\text{Rock}\cdot g\cdot(h - y)
E_\text{TOT} = E_\text{pot} + E_\text{kin} = m_\text{Rock}\,g\,y + m_\text{Rock}\,g\,(h - y) = m_\text{Rock}\,g\,(y + h - y) = m_\text{Rock}\cdot g\cdot h

So E_\text{TOT} = \text{const}: the y cancels, the total is the same at every height.

At III (y = 0): only kinetic energy, with the full drop height:

E_\text{kin} = m_\text{Rock}\cdot\frac{v_\text{Rock}^2}{2} = m_\text{Rock}\cdot\frac{\left(\sqrt{2gh}\right)^2}{2} = m_\text{Rock}\cdot g\cdot h = E_\text{TOT}
Symbols
  • m_\text{Rock} — mass of the rock (kg); g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}
  • h — starting height above the floor (m); y — current height (m), y up, zero level at the floor
  • v_\text{Rock} — speed of the rock at height y (m/s); h - y — the drop height so far
  • E_\text{pot}, E_\text{kin} — potential and kinetic energy (J); E_\text{TOT} — their sum (J)

The lecture runs the argument "backwards": it takes the speed from kinematics and shows that the sum comes out constant. In practice it runs the other way: assume E_\text{TOT} = \text{const} and get the speed without any kinematics, \tfrac12 m v^2 = m g\,(h - y). That route works for any path, not only straight down, which kinematics can't do.

Common mistake — the mass matters

Heavier rocks have more energy, so it's tempting to think they reach the floor faster. Every term carries m: \tfrac12 m v^2 = m g h, the mass cancels, v = \sqrt{2gh} for every mass. A heavier rock has more kinetic energy at the floor, not more speed.

2 Two slides of the same height, and the cycloid ramp

Lecture: p. 7 top ("From an energy perspective") · Giancoli §8-4

Pasted figure: two water slides start at the same height h and end at the same point. Paul is on the upper slide (S_P), which starts flat and drops late; Corinne on the lower one (S_C), which drops steeply at the start. Bar charts show PE and KE at the start (I), part-way (II) and at the bottom (III).

The pasted figure. The bars on the right show the energy at three moments: Jeanne turns her potential energy U into kinetic energy K earlier (her slide drops steeply first), so she is faster most of the way, but at the bottom both have the same K. The book writes U, K for the lecture's E_\text{pot}, E_\text{kin}. (Giancoli Fig. 8-9)

From an energy perspective (board):

\text{I:}\ \ E_{\text{pot},P} = E_{\text{pot},C}, \qquad \text{III:}\ \ E_{\text{kin},P} = E_{\text{kin},C}
Symbols
  • E_{\text{pot},P}, E_{\text{pot},C} — Paul's and Corinne's potential energy at the start (J); per kilogram the same, g h, because the height is the same
  • E_{\text{kin},P}, E_{\text{kin},C} — their kinetic energies at the bottom (J)
  • I, III — start and bottom of the slides

Both start at rest from the same height, and (no friction) only gravity does work on them. All of m g h becomes \tfrac12 m v^2 at the bottom, so both arrive with the same speed v = \sqrt{2gh}, whatever the shape of the slide. The shape doesn't enter the energy balance at all.

Who arrives first is a different question, about time, and energy alone can't answer it. Corinne's slide drops steeply at once, so she is lower than Paul at every moment, has converted more potential energy into speed, and is faster than him all the way: she arrives first. The board notes the trade-off: you want to build up speed early (a steep start, sketched as a curve that drops at once), but you also want the slide length to be short. A very steep start followed by a long flat run wastes time on the extra length. The best compromise is a cycloid, the curve traced by a point on a rolling wheel; the embedded video "Cycloid Ramp" (p. 7, a race between balls on differently shaped ramps) shows it winning.

Beyond the lecture (no matching Giancoli section)

The curve of fastest descent between two points is called the brachistochrone ("shortest time"); Johann Bernoulli posed the problem in 1696, and its solution is the cycloid. Finding it needs the calculus of variations, well beyond this course; for the exam the point is only that speed depends on height, time on shape.

Problem-solving steps — speed at a lower point, any path
  1. Check that no friction acts (or that it can be neglected); otherwise see section 4.
  2. Take the zero level at the lower point; the start is h above it.
  3. \tfrac12 m v_2^2 = \tfrac12 m v_1^2 + m g h; from rest, v_2 = \sqrt{2gh}.
  4. Don't use energy to compare times: that needs the shape of the path.

3 Gravity and a spring: the bungee jumper

Lecture: p. 5 bottom – p. 7 top ("2nd example: Bungee jumper") · Giancoli §8-4

Pasted figure (three moments): (a) the jumper stands on the platform at height h above the water (y = 0, y up); (b) after falling freely 15 m, the cord ("15 m", marked Y_0) is just straight; (c) at the lowest point the cord is stretched by "\Delta y = ?" and the jumper just reaches the water.

The same physics in a simpler setting: a ball falls from height h onto a spring (a, b) and compresses it by Y (c). Gravity's potential energy turns into kinetic energy and then into spring energy, exactly as for the bungee rope. (Giancoli Fig. 8-13)

Given (board): k = 50\ \mathrm{N/m}, m = 100\ \mathrm{kg}, g \approx 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}, unstretched cord length 15 m. The platform height h is unknown ("UNKNOWN"): how high must it be so that the jumper doesn't hit the water? The cord is treated as a spring that acts only once it is stretched; air resistance and the cord's mass are neglected, so energy is conserved: E_{(a)} = E_{(b)} = E_{(c)}.

The energy at each moment (zero level: the water):

  • (a) at rest on the platform: E_\text{pot} = m\,g\,h.
  • (b) after 15 m of free fall: E_\text{pot} = m\,g\,(h - 15\ \mathrm m), \ E_\text{kin} = m\,\frac{\left(\sqrt{2g\cdot 15\ \mathrm m}\right)^2}{2} = m\cdot 150\ \frac{\mathrm m^2}{\mathrm s^2}.
  • (c) at the water (h = 0 written on the board for the jumper's height there): E_\text{kin} = m\,\frac{v_F^2}{2}, \ E_\text{spring} = k\,\frac{(h - 15\ \mathrm m)^2}{2}, since the cord is stretched by everything beyond its 15 m.
\underbrace{m\,g\,h}_{E(a)} = \underbrace{m\,g\,(h - 15\ \mathrm m) + m\cdot 150\ \tfrac{\mathrm m^2}{\mathrm s^2}}_{E(b)} = \underbrace{m\,\frac{v_F^2}{2} + k\,\frac{(h - 15\ \mathrm m)^2}{2}}_{E(c)}
Symbols
  • m — mass of the jumper (kg); g \approx 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2} (rounded in the lecture)
  • h — height of the platform above the water (m), the unknown
  • 15\ \mathrm m — the cord's unstretched length; (h - 15\ \mathrm m) — its stretch when the jumper reaches the water (m)
  • k — the cord's spring constant (N/m); E_\text{spring} = \tfrac12 k\,(\text{stretch})^2 — its potential energy (J), from 11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 8 Potential energy
  • v_F — the jumper's speed at the lowest point (m/s)

m\cdot150\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2} is the kinetic energy after 15 m of free fall: v^2 = 2g\cdot15\ \mathrm m = 300\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}, and half of it times m. Check: E(a) = E(b), because m g h = m g h - m g\cdot15 + m\cdot150 and m g\cdot 15 = m\cdot150 with g = 10 ✓.

New reference height. The algebra gets simpler if the zero level is moved to the lowest point and the unknown is the stretch \Delta y instead of h (board: "pick new reference height \Delta y"). Then at (b) the jumper is \Delta y above the zero level:

E_{(b)} = m\,g\,\Delta y + 100\ \mathrm{kg}\cdot 150\ \frac{\mathrm m^2}{\mathrm s^2} = M g\,\Delta y + 15\,000\ \mathrm J, \qquad E_{(c)} = m\,\frac{v_F^2}{2} + k\,\frac{\Delta y^2}{2}
Symbols
  • \Delta y — stretch of the cord at the lowest point (m) = the height of point (b) above the lowest point
  • M — the same mass m (the board switches letters)

The speed at the lowest point is zero. The board crosses out the m\,v_F^2/2 term: "v_F = 0\ \mathrm{m/s} — NOBODY NOTICED". At the lowest point the jumper turns around, so the speed there is zero. The earlier boxed note "v_F = \sqrt{2gh}" is the free-fall speed and does not hold here (the cord brakes the fall); the remark records that this slip went unnoticed at first. With v_F = 0:

\begin{aligned} m\,g\,\Delta y + 15\,000\ \mathrm J &= k\,\frac{\Delta y^2}{2} && \text{(}E_{(b)} = E_{(c)}\text{)} \\ -\frac{k}{2}\,\Delta y^2 + m\,g\,\Delta y + 15\,000\ \mathrm J &= 0 && \text{(bring everything to one side: } a x^2 + b x + c = 0) \\ \Delta y_{1,2} &= \frac{-b \pm\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} && \text{(}a = -\tfrac k2 = -25\ \tfrac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm m},\ b = m g = 1000\ \mathrm N,\ c = 15\,000\ \mathrm J) \\ &= \frac{-1000\ \mathrm N \pm\sqrt{(1000\ \mathrm N)^2 + 4\cdot 25\ \tfrac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm m}\cdot 15\,000\ \mathrm J}}{-50\ \tfrac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm m}} && \\ &= \frac{-1000\ \mathrm N \pm\sqrt{2.5\cdot10^{6}\ \mathrm N^2}}{-50\ \tfrac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm m}} = \frac{-10^3\ \mathrm N \pm 1.58\cdot10^3\ \mathrm N}{-50\ \tfrac{\mathrm N}{\mathrm m}} && \text{(}\sqrt{2.5} \approx 1.58\text{)} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • a, b, c — coefficients of the quadratic in \Delta y; \Delta y_{1,2} — its two roots (m)
  • units: \mathrm{N}/(\mathrm{N/m}) = \mathrm m ✓; inside the root \mathrm{N^2} and \mathrm{N/m}\cdot\mathrm{J} = \mathrm{N/m}\cdot\mathrm{N\,m} = \mathrm{N^2} ✓

The "+" root gives \Delta y = \frac{+580}{-50} = -11.6\ \mathrm m, a negative stretch: rejected ("REJECT"). The "−" root:

\Delta y = \frac{-10^3\ \mathrm N - 1.58\cdot10^3\ \mathrm N}{-50\ \mathrm{N/m}} = \frac{2580}{50}\ \mathrm m \approx 51.6\ \mathrm m, \qquad h > 51.6\ \mathrm m + 15\ \mathrm m = 66.6\ \mathrm m

So the platform must be at least 66.6 m above the water; the board recommends h \approx 72–75\ \mathrm m, a margin of about 10 % for the jumper's height, a heavier jumper and an imperfect cord.

Unclear (p. 6): "\sqrt{1.5\cdot10^{6}\ \mathrm N^2}"

The second line under the root writes 1.5\cdot10^{6}. The discriminant is 10^{6} + 1.5\cdot10^{6} = 2.5\cdot10^{6}\ \mathrm{N^2}, which the next line uses (\sqrt{2.5} \approx 1.58). The "1.5" is a copying slip; the result 51.6 m is correct for the given numbers.

Unclear (p. 6–7): the "side quest" and "FROM EXP"

The board asks: "Side quest: what (amount by %) was the mistake of the simplification?" It doesn't say which simplification. The most likely one is g \approx 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}: with g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2} the same steps give \Delta y = 50.8\ \mathrm m and h > 65.8\ \mathrm m, so the rounding overestimates the needed height by about 1.2 % (on the safe side). Other simplifications (massless cord, no air resistance, the jumper as a point) can't be quantified with the given data. "FROM EXP" under the boxed h > 66.6\ \mathrm m is not readable with certainty, most likely "from the expression" or "from experience". Ask in the tutorial.

Why does the quadratic have two roots, and what is the other one?

The energy equation doesn't know that a cord can only pull. It treats the cord as a spring that would also push when compressed. The second root, \Delta y = -11.6\ \mathrm m, is a turning point 11.6 m above point (b), where the cord would have to be compressed by 11.6 m (3.4 m below the platform). A cord can't be compressed; it simply goes slack, so this root has no meaning: reject it.

Worked example — how much rope for a given bridge?

A 70 kg jumper on a 50 m high bridge, cord k = 60\ \mathrm{N/m}. How long may the unstretched cord be? (Use g = 9.81.)

  1. Unknown: cord length L; at the lowest point (the water) the stretch is 50 - L.
  2. Energy, zero level at the water, both ends at rest: m g\cdot 50 = \tfrac12 k\,(50 - L)^2.
  3. Solve: (50 - L)^2 = \frac{2\cdot 70\cdot 9.81\cdot 50}{60} = 1144.5\ \mathrm{m^2}, so 50 - L = 33.8\ \mathrm m, L = 16.2\ \mathrm m.
  4. Check: \tfrac12\cdot 60\cdot 33.8^2 = 34\,300\ \mathrm J = 70\cdot9.81\cdot50 ✓. A shorter cord is safer.
Problem-solving steps — gravity and a spring together
  1. Draw the key moments: start, the moment the spring/cord starts to act, the turning point.
  2. Fix one zero level for gravity (the lowest point is often simplest) and measure the spring's stretch from its relaxed length.
  3. At a turning point the speed is zero.
  4. Set the total energies equal: m g y_1 + \tfrac12 m v_1^2 + \tfrac12 k x_1^2 = m g y_2 + \tfrac12 m v_2^2 + \tfrac12 k x_2^2.
  5. A quadratic appears: keep the physical root (positive stretch), reject the other.

4 Energy with friction: the ramp

Lecture: p. 7 bottom – p. 8 top · Giancoli §8-5, §8-6

Board, p. 7: a block m at height H (I) slides down a slope with "\mu \approx 0" to the bottom (II), then along a flat floor with "\mu \neq 0" (III); the distance travelled on the floor is x, with the note "x has an upper limit!".

The slope is frictionless, the floor is not. Friction is not conservative, so the mechanical energy is no longer constant; the energy it removes becomes heat. The total energy still is constant, if the heat is counted.

At I (rest, height H): E_\text{pot} = m\cdot g\cdot H.

At II (bottom of the slope, frictionless so far): all of it is kinetic, at the highest speed:

m\,g\,H = \frac{m\cdot v_\text{max}^2}{2}

At III (after the distance x on the floor): part is still kinetic, part has become heat. The heat equals the work done against friction, force times distance:

E_\text{kin} = \frac{m\cdot v(x)^2}{2}, \qquad E_\text{HEAT} = F_F\cdot x, \qquad E_\text{TOT} = \frac{m\,v(x)^2}{2} + F_F\cdot x

On the flat floor F_N = m\cdot g and F_F = \mu\cdot F_N = \mu\cdot m\cdot g (sliding friction, 9 Free-Body Diagrams and Friction › 2 Friction: sliding and static):

E_\text{TOT} = \frac{m\,v(x)^2}{2} + \mu\,m\,g\cdot x = m\,g\,H
Symbols
  • m — mass of the block (kg); H — starting height (m); g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}
  • v_\text{max} — speed at the bottom of the slope (m/s); v(x) — speed after sliding x on the floor (m/s)
  • F_F — sliding friction force on the floor (N); \mu — its (sliding) coefficient, \mu_d in earlier notes; F_N — normal force (N)
  • E_\text{HEAT} — energy turned into heat by friction (J) = the work done against friction
  • E_\text{TOT} — total energy, mechanical plus heat (J), equal to the starting m g H

The upper limit of x. The block stops when all its kinetic energy is gone, v(x) = 0. Then \mu\,m\,g\,x = m\,g\,H, so (board) "if \mu x = H":

\boxed{\,x_\text{max} = \frac{H}{\mu}\,}

Mass and g cancel: a block from 3 m with \mu = 0.25 slides 12 m, whatever it weighs. The general rule, which the lecture applies here, is the work–energy principle with friction: the starting mechanical energy equals the final mechanical energy plus the heat, E_{\text{kin},1} + E_{\text{pot},1} = E_{\text{kin},2} + E_{\text{pot},2} + F_F\cdot\ell for a constant friction force over a path length \ell.

Worked example — speed part-way along the floor

H = 3\ \mathrm m, \mu = 0.25. How fast is the block after x = 6\ \mathrm m on the floor?

  1. Energy balance: \tfrac12 m v^2 = m g H - \mu m g x, the mass cancels: v = \sqrt{2g\,(H - \mu x)}.
  2. Numbers: v = \sqrt{2\cdot 9.81\cdot(3 - 1.5)} = 5.42\ \mathrm{m/s} (at the bottom of the slope it was \sqrt{2\cdot9.81\cdot3} = 7.67\ \mathrm{m/s}).
  3. Check: at x = 12\ \mathrm m = H/\mu the bracket is zero, v = 0 ✓; half the friction distance has removed half the energy.
Common mistake — friction in E_\text{pot}, or the heat with the wrong sign

Friction has no potential energy (its work depends on the path, 11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 8 Potential energy). Its effect enters as an extra term F_F\cdot\ell on the "after" side, energy that left the mechanical system. Putting it on the "before" side or with a minus sign makes the block speed up from friction.

Problem-solving steps — energy with friction
  1. Mark start and end; choose the zero level of height.
  2. Find the friction force on each part of the path (F_F = \mu F_N; on flat ground F_N = mg, on an incline mg\cos\alpha).
  3. Write E_{\text{kin},1} + E_{\text{pot},1} = E_{\text{kin},2} + E_{\text{pot},2} + \sum F_F\,\ell (heat on the "after" side).
  4. Stopping distance: set E_{\text{kin},2} = 0.
  5. Check: with \mu = 0 you must get back the frictionless result.

5 Units of energy and power; the calorie

Lecture: p. 7 middle · Giancoli §8-8 (calorie: Chapter 19, not downloaded yet)

Power is energy (or work) per time, \text{POWER} = \frac{\text{ENERGY or WORK}}{\text{TIME}} (11 Gravitational Field, Work, Kinetic and Potential Energy › 10 Power). The board collects the units:

[P] = \frac{\mathrm J}{\mathrm s} = \frac{\mathrm{N\,m}}{\mathrm s} = \mathrm W, \qquad [E] = \mathrm J = \mathrm{N\,m} = \mathrm{W\,s},\ \ \text{also cal}
Symbols
  • P — power (W, watt); E — energy (J, joule)
  • \mathrm{W\,s} — watt-second: one watt for one second = 1 J
  • cal — calorie (see below)

kWh … not an SI unit. The kilowatt-hour on the electricity bill is the energy of 1 kW for one hour: 1\ \mathrm{kWh} = 1000\ \mathrm W\cdot3600\ \mathrm s = 3.6\cdot10^{6}\ \mathrm J. It is a unit of energy, not power, built from the non-SI unit hour.

The calorie (board): 1 cal is the energy to heat up 1 g of water by 1 °C or 1 K. 1\ \mathrm{cal} \mathrel{\hat=} 4.184\ \mathrm J, the "heat capacity of water"; 1\ \mathrm{kcal} = 1000\ \mathrm{cal}. (A temperature difference of 1 °C is the same as 1 K, 1 Physical Quantities and the SI System.) Food labels give kcal: a 250 kcal snack is about 1.05\cdot10^{6}\ \mathrm J, enough energy, in principle, to lift a 75 kg person by 1.05\cdot10^{6}/(75\cdot9.81) \approx 1400\ \mathrm m. The body converts only about a quarter of food energy into mechanical work, the rest becomes heat.

Common mistake — kW and kWh

kW is a power (how fast), kWh an energy (how much). A 2 kW kettle running for 3 minutes uses 2\ \mathrm{kW}\cdot0.05\ \mathrm h = 0.1\ \mathrm{kWh} = 360\ \mathrm{kJ}. "kW per hour" is not a unit of anything here.

6 Linear momentum

Lecture: p. 8 ("Linear momentum & collisions") · Giancoli §9-1

Why a new quantity. Board sketch: a car drives into a wall. With F = m\cdot a, at impact the car has a large negative acceleration -a. The collision lasts a very short time: a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} with \Delta t \to 0 grows toward -\infty. The force during the impact is huge, changes very fast and is practically never known, so Newton's second law in the form F = m a is hard to use for a collision.

Instead of forces → linear momentum:

\vec p = m\cdot\vec v
Symbols
  • \vec p — linear momentum of the body (kg·m/s), a vector in the direction of the velocity
  • m — mass (kg); \vec v — velocity (m/s)

The general form of Newton's second law, \vec F = \frac{\mathrm d\vec p}{\mathrm dt}, was introduced in 8 Newton's Laws and Forces › 4 Momentum: the general form of axiom 2. Momentum is what a force changes: the longer and the harder it pushes, the more momentum it adds. In a collision the force is unknown, but the momenta before and after are not; the next section shows how they are linked.

Unclear (p. 8): "\Delta a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}"

The board seems to write \Delta a on the left. The acceleration is a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} (no \Delta on a); the stroke before it may be a stray mark or a sloppy "a". The argument (\Delta t \to 0 makes a \to -\infty) is the same either way.

Beyond the lecture (Giancoli §9-3)

The book makes the crash argument quantitative with the impulse: integrating \vec F = \mathrm d\vec p/\mathrm dt over the short impact time gives \int\vec F\,\mathrm dt = \Delta\vec p. The momentum change is fixed by the speeds before and after; a longer stopping time (crumple zone, airbag) therefore means a smaller average force. A 1000 kg car stopping from 15 m/s in 0.1 s needs an average force of 1.5\cdot10^{5}\ \mathrm N; stretching the stop to 0.3 s cuts it to a third.

7 Conservation of momentum

Lecture: p. 8 ("From Newton's third law") · Giancoli §9-2

Board, from Newton's third law: \vec p = m\cdot\vec v, \vec p momentum is also conserved.

When two bodies collide, m_1 pushes on m_2 and m_2 pushes back with the opposite force at every moment of the contact (reaction principle): \vec F_{12} = -\vec F_{21}. Each force changes its body's momentum, \vec F = \mathrm d\vec p/\mathrm dt:

During a collision, A pushes B with \vec F and B pushes A with -\vec F, at every instant. Equal and opposite forces for the same time change the two momenta by equal and opposite amounts, so the total stays the same. (Giancoli Fig. 9-4)

Conservation of momentum in use: car A rolls into car B at rest and they couple. Before: p = m_A v_A. After: both move together with v', and (m_A + m_B)v' = m_A v_A gives the common speed. (Giancoli Fig. 9-5)

\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm d\vec p_1}{\mathrm dt} &= \vec F_{12}, \quad \frac{\mathrm d\vec p_2}{\mathrm dt} = \vec F_{21} && \text{(second law for each body; only the contact forces act)} \\ \frac{\mathrm d\vec p_1}{\mathrm dt} + \frac{\mathrm d\vec p_2}{\mathrm dt} &= \vec F_{12} + \vec F_{21} = \vec 0 && \text{(add; third law)} \\ \vec p_1 + \vec p_2 &= \text{const} && \text{(a quantity with zero rate of change is constant)} \end{aligned}
Symbols
  • \vec p_1 = m_1\vec v_1, \vec p_2 = m_2\vec v_2 — momenta of the two bodies (kg·m/s)
  • \vec F_{12} — force on body 1 from body 2 (N); \vec F_{21} — force on body 2 from body 1 (N)

Whatever momentum one body loses, the other gains, at every instant. Over the whole collision, before (unprimed) and after (primed):

\sum\vec p = \text{preserved}: \qquad m_1\cdot\vec v_1 + m_2\cdot\vec v_2 = m_1\cdot\vec v_1\,' + m_2\cdot\vec v_2\,'
Symbols
  • \vec v_1, \vec v_2 — velocities just before the collision (m/s); \vec v_1\,', \vec v_2\,' — just after (m/s)
  • m_1, m_2 — the two masses (kg)

Board sketches (axes: x to the right, y up): (1) head-on: m_1 moves right with v_1, m_2 moves left with v_2; after the collision v_1' points left and v_2' right. (2) catching up: both move to the right, v_1 > v_2, so m_1 runs into m_2 from behind.

The equation is a vector equation; for motion along a line it becomes one equation in the x components, with signs. In sketch (1), v_2 points to the left, so its x component is negative. The condition behind it: no net external force on the pair. During a short collision external forces like friction from the road are small compared with the contact forces and act only for that short time, so momentum is conserved across the impact itself, even if not before or after.

Common mistake — adding speeds instead of velocities

In the head-on case, m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 with both speeds positive overcounts. With x to the right, a body moving left has a negative velocity component: m_1 v_1 - m_2\lvert v_2\rvert. Fix the axis first, give every velocity its sign, and read the signs of the results as directions.

Intuition

Momentum is like money that two bodies pass between themselves: the contact forces move it from one to the other, never create or destroy it. Energy is like money that can also be spent on heat and deformation, so the kinetic energy of the two bodies need not add up afterwards.

8 Collisions: elastic and inelastic

Lecture: p. 8 · Giancoli §9-4 to §9-6

Pasted figure: two balls m_1 and m_2 before, during and after a collision, with their momenta \vec p_1, \vec p_2 before and \vec p_1\,', \vec p_2\,' after.

Momentum is conserved in every collision (section 7). The kinetic energy is what distinguishes the types (board):

  • Elastic collision: kinetic energy is preserved, \tfrac12 m_1 v_1^2 + \tfrac12 m_2 v_2^2 = \tfrac12 m_1 v_1'^2 + \tfrac12 m_2 v_2'^2. The bodies bounce off each other without lasting deformation (billiard balls, steel balls, nearly).
  • (Fully) inelastic collision: deformation, both objects stick together. They move on with one common velocity, \vec v_1\,' = \vec v_2\,' = \vec v\,'. Kinetic energy is lost to deformation and heat; the total energy is still conserved.
  • Partially elastic / inelastic collision: in reality, collisions lie between the two: the bodies separate, but some kinetic energy is lost.

For the fully inelastic case, the momentum equation alone gives the result. With \vec v_1\,' = \vec v_2\,' = \vec v\,':

m_1\vec v_1 + m_2\vec v_2 = (m_1 + m_2)\,\vec v\,' \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \vec v\,' = \frac{m_1\vec v_1 + m_2\vec v_2}{m_1 + m_2}
Symbols
  • \vec v\,' — common velocity of the two stuck bodies after the collision (m/s)
  • m_1, m_2, \vec v_1, \vec v_2 — as above

The common velocity is the mass-weighted average of the two velocities, the same weighting as the centre of mass in 3 Center of Mass: it is in fact the velocity of the centre of mass, which a collision doesn't change.

Worked example — two cars stick together

A 1200 kg car at 15 m/s (to the right) hits a 900 kg car coming the other way at 10 m/s; they lock together.

  1. Axis: x to the right: v_1 = +15\ \mathrm{m/s}, v_2 = -10\ \mathrm{m/s}.
  2. Momentum: v' = \dfrac{1200\cdot15 + 900\cdot(-10)}{2100}\ \mathrm{m/s} = \dfrac{9000}{2100}\ \mathrm{m/s} = +4.29\ \mathrm{m/s}, to the right.
  3. Kinetic energy: before \tfrac12\cdot1200\cdot15^2 + \tfrac12\cdot900\cdot10^2 = 180\ \mathrm{kJ}; after \tfrac12\cdot2100\cdot4.29^2 = 19.3\ \mathrm{kJ}. About 89 % goes into deformation and heat.
  4. Check: the heavier, faster car wins the direction ✓; \lvert v'\rvert lies between the two speeds ✓.
Problem-solving steps — collisions
  1. Choose the system (both bodies) and check that external forces are negligible during the impact.
  2. Choose the x axis (often along one initial velocity) and give every velocity its sign.
  3. Write momentum conservation, one equation per direction: m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = m_1 v_1' + m_2 v_2'.
  4. Add what the collision type gives: stuck together → v_1' = v_2'; elastic → kinetic energy conserved as a second equation.
  5. Check the signs (directions) and that the kinetic energy did not increase.
Connection

Momentum conservation is how a robot's contact with an object (a grasp, a kick in robot football, a collision with an obstacle) is modelled when the contact force is too short and stiff to simulate step by step. The conservation laws of this and the last lecture (energy, momentum) are the two shortcuts that replace force-by-force calculations throughout mechanics.
